title: Goosebumps are the same reflex that fluffs up a frightened cat's fur
body: Each hair in your skin has a tiny **arrector pili** muscle at its base. When the sympathetic nervous system, the branch that runs the fight-or-flight response, fires them, the hairs stand on end and the skin around them puckers into goosebumps. In furry animals the raised coat traps air for insulation and makes the animal look bigger, as in a frightened cat or a stressed mouse. Human body hair is too sparse for either job, so many consider the reflex vestigial, yet cold, fear, strong emotion and even music still trigger it.

slides.question: Which muscles raise the hairs in goosebumps?
slides.explanation: A tiny arrector pili muscle sits at the base of each hair. When sympathetic nerves fire them, the hairs stand up and the skin puckers around them.

left.label: Furry animals
left.text: Raised fur traps air for insulation and makes a frightened cat, chimpanzee or mouse look bigger to a rival.

right.label: Humans
right.text: Our sparse hair traps little air and scares nobody, so many scientists call the reflex vestigial.

slides.clue: A formal medical word for goosebumps, also known as piloerection
slides.detail: Other names are the pilomotor reflex and cutis anserina, Latin for goose skin.

slides.heading: Why goose?
slides.text: The name comes from the look of a plucked goose: its feathers grow from pores much like hair follicles, leaving bumps behind. Nobody is sure why English picked the goose; other languages reach for hens, chickens, ducks or even ants.
